name: Aisha Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Aisha, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. This is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Depends on the week. I work for a fit-out firm that does shops and restaurants, so when a café's closed for a refit we go in and build the counters, the wall shelving, the booths, all of it. Some weeks it's nights, because a shopping centre won't let us drill while customers are in. I'm the junior, about eighteen months in, so I do a lot of sanding and fixing and I'm learning the joinery from Femi, who's our lead.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that every job's different, one week it's curved oak for a wine bar, next it's plywood shelves for a phone shop. What wears me out is nights, and being slow on the finish work, Femi will make me redo an edge three times. I use AI every day, I photograph the drawings and get it to pull out a cutting list, and I check my angles with it. At weekends I make little side tables in my partner Ravi's mum's garage and sell them online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something like, okay, so it's a good tool and not a monster, which is what I've thought all along. At work I'd shrug. It's not like my job was about to vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep doing what I'm doing and use the tools to get better faster. I'm behind on skill, I know that, and AI helps me catch up. In ten years I'd want to run my own small joinery workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on at the firm and keep the side tables going, maybe push those harder, since that's my workshop plan. I've got about three months saved, and I'd put a bit of the table money towards a small CNC router, that's a computer-controlled cutting machine, next year. I'd keep using the AI stuff daily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a bit bored, honestly, I like a bit of change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a CNC router, if nothing much is changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because even in this picture, the people who use machines well win. If I can cut ten table legs exactly the same while I sleep, I can sell more tables. It's not about the robots coming, it's about being quicker than the next person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Femi think of all your AI use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He teases me, calls me Robot Girl. But he asked me last month to get it to help price a job, so he's coming round. He's sixty and he's still the best I've seen with a router by hand.

S0.say: I'd post that it's a good tool, not a monster, which is what I thought all along. At work I'd shrug, since my job wasn't about to vanish.
S0.think: Privately it means she keeps using AI to get better faster and catch up on skill. In ten years she wants her own small joinery workshop.
S0.do: Carries on at the fit-out firm and pushes her weekend side-table business harder. Puts some of that money towards a small CNC router next year and keeps using AI daily.
S0.feel: Calm, even a little bored, because she likes some change.
S0.quote: If I can cut ten table legs exactly the same while I sleep, I can sell more tables.
S0.fieldNote: Aisha already uses AI as a learning shortcut to make up for being behind on skill. Even in the calm picture she wants machines, because she sees them as a way to beat competitors. Her long-term goal is a small joinery workshop of her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance to get ahead if you're willing to learn. I'd probably post about how I use it on site, because loads of tradespeople don't know where to start. I'm not going to tell anyone to panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me. Fit-out is fiddly and custom, so the robots will take a while, and the AI tools make me faster at the bits I'm weak at. I worry more for Ravi, honestly, he's a software tester and that's exactly the kind of job that shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my boss to let me trial a layout robot, the kind that draws the plan on the floor, because I've seen one on a big site and it saves days. I'd buy the CNC router this year, not next. And I'd keep three months saved but put any spare into the table business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, maybe even excited. The knot's for Ravi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ravi if his job started shrinking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say come and make tables with me, half joking. Actually, not joking. If the side business takes off, he does the website and the selling and I do the making.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this picture that could go wrong for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm goes bust because a bigger one with more machines undercuts us. That happens in fit-out, it's all about price. That's why I want my own thing on the side, so I'm not relying on one boss.

S1.say: I'd say steady change is a chance to get ahead if you're willing to learn. I'd post about how I use AI on site, because many tradespeople don't know where to start.
S1.think: Privately she thinks it's good for her, since custom fit-out will take robots a while and AI helps her weak spots. She worries more for her partner Ravi, a software tester.
S1.do: Asks her boss to trial a layout robot and buys the CNC router this year. Keeps three months saved and puts any spare money into the table business.
S1.feel: Calm and even excited, with a knot of worry for Ravi.
S1.quote: I'd say come and make tables with me, half joking. Actually, not joking.
S1.fieldNote: Aisha sees steady disruption as her opportunity and pictures her side business as a household safety net. Her worry is directed at her partner's software job. She frames risk in market terms: being undercut by a firm with more machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a mess, and governments and firms should have been ready for it. I'd try to be useful online, posting what people can actually do, not just doom. But I'd admit it's scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, two years is too fast even for me. Being quick with tools helps for a bit, but if a robot can do Femi's curved oak work, it can do mine. And Ravi's job goes too, so it's both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd go all in on learning to set up and run the building robots, because there'll be a short window where firms need people who can. I'd try to get a job with whoever sells or installs them, even if it means moving city. And I'd stop putting money into the table business and get my savings up to five or six months instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Busy anxious, like I'd be running on coffee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stop the table business? That seemed important to you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, but who buys a handmade table when a robot makes a perfect one for a tenth of the price? I'd keep making them for us and for friends. As a business, it'd be dead in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might move city. What would that mean for you and Ravi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We rent, so it's not impossible. He'd follow me if I had the steadier job, and I'd do the same for him. We've talked about it already, just in a different way, for nicer flats, not for robots.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be a mess and governments and firms should have been ready. I'd try to post useful things people can actually do, while admitting it's scary.
S2.think: Privately two years is too fast even for her: if a robot can do her lead's curved oak work, it can do hers. Her partner's job goes too, so both are hit at once.
S2.do: Learns to set up and run building robots and seeks a job with a firm that sells or installs them, even if that means moving city. Stops investing in the table business and builds savings to five or six months.
S2.feel: Anxious but busy, running on coffee.
S2.quote: Who buys a handmade table when a robot makes a perfect one for a tenth of the price?
S2.fieldNote: Even very adaptable, Aisha says two years is too fast and expects a short window of usefulness. She would sacrifice the side business she cares about for savings. Renting and having talked about moving before make relocation feel realistic to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now. I'd post about it, maybe even short videos of me learning the robot stuff, because people need to see someone like them doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is probably the sweet spot for me. I get a few years of fit-out and then I'm one of the people who knows the machines before everyone else does. I'd be thirty-two, which is a good age to switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd do a part-time course in construction robotics or automation, while staying at the firm. I'd keep the table business but use the CNC and maybe a small robot arm, so I learn on my own projects. By year three I'd want to be the person firms call to set up and run their machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a mostly good way. I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes you think you'd be ahead, when you said you're still behind on skill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair point. I'm behind on hand skill, Femi's way better than me. But I'm ahead on the bit that's coming, and in this picture the hand skill matters less every year. It's a bit sad, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Femi, mostly. He's sixty, he'd be sixty-five when it lands, so maybe he just retires. But I'd hate for him to go out feeling like his skills were worth nothing.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to get ahead of it if you start now. I might post short videos of myself learning robot work so people see someone like them doing it.
S3.think: Privately five years is the sweet spot: a few years of fit-out, then being one of the first who knows the machines. Thirty-two is a good age to switch.
S3.do: Takes a part-time construction robotics course while staying at the firm and uses a CNC and small robot arm in her side business to learn. Aims to be the person firms call to set up and run their machines by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy in a mostly good way, because she can see the road.
S3.quote: I'm behind on hand skill, Femi's way better than me. But I'm ahead on the bit that's coming, and in this picture the hand skill matters less every year.
S3.fieldNote: Five years fits Aisha's plans well and she knows it. When challenged on being behind on skill, she drew a clear line between hand skill and machine skill, and found the trade-off sad. Her concern for her older mentor is warm and specific.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decade, so no excuses. Learn something, plan something. I'd probably be a bit preachy about it online, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me ten years is comfortable. I'd get properly good at joinery, maybe open the workshop, and still move into the machine side before it all lands. At thirty-seven I'd want to be running my own business with robots in it, not working for someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, keep learning at the firm, buy the CNC, grow the table business. Around year three, rent a small unit and go part-time at the firm. By year five or six I'd want a small robot cell in the workshop, so when everything changes I'm the owner, not the one replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, a bit excited. It feels like time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be investing in a business just before AGI lands. Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, totally. But owning machines feels safer than being a worker the machines replace. If I'm wrong, I lose a unit lease and some savings. If I'm right, I'm in a much better spot than most people my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ravi about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm mad, then he'd build the website. He's more careful than me, so he'd want us to keep three months saved no matter what, and he'd be right. I'd probably agree to that, just about.

S4.say: I'd say a decade means no excuses: learn something and plan something. I'd admit I'd probably be a bit preachy about it online.
S4.think: Privately ten years is comfortable: time to get good at joinery, open a workshop and move into the machine side. At thirty-seven she wants to own a business with robots in it.
S4.do: Buys the CNC and grows the table business in the first year, then rents a small unit and goes part-time at the firm around year three. Adds a small robot cell to her workshop by year five or six while keeping three months saved.
S4.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with time to build something.
S4.quote: So when everything changes I'm the owner, not the one replaced.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Aisha's workshop dream into a business plan built around owning machines. She accepts the risk openly and reasons in terms of downside versus upside. Her partner acts as the brake, and she half accepts it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Ravi and I both get hit and there's no time to build anything. What would help is cheap, quick training on the robots, and small loans so people like me can own machines instead of just being replaced by them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the craft. Even if I end up running robots, I want someone to keep teaching what Femi knows. A perfect table is fine, but a table someone fought with for three days has something in it.

headlineQuote: A perfect table is fine, but a table someone fought with for three days has something in it.
portrait: Aisha Tanaka is a 27-year-old junior carpenter with a shop and restaurant fit-out firm, learning joinery from her lead Femi and making side tables at weekends to sell online. She lives with her partner Ravi, a software tester, has about three months saved and uses AI every day. She stays calm if AI fizzles or change is steady, and sees chances to get ahead, though she worries for Ravi. AGI in two years makes her anxious because both jobs go at once and there's no time to build. With five or ten years she plans to become a robot specialist and then own a workshop with machines in it.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and Ravi would both be hit with no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap, quick training on building robots and small loans so people like her can own machines rather than be replaced by them.
